clue_1: Born in Sydney in 2001, he played his junior football for the Berala Bears and St Johns Eagles, and as a teenager was signed by one NRL club and then a second, without ever playing a first-grade game for either of them
clue_2: A powerfully built outside back comfortable on the wing, in the centres or at fullback, he is known for the hard metres he grinds out bringing the ball off his own line, regularly finishing among the competition's leaders for tackle busts
clue_3: He scored a hat-trick against Newcastle in 2022, one of the very clubs that had earlier let him go, and crossed for a second career treble against the Gold Coast three seasons later
clue_4: A genuine fan favourite, he became a key outside back in the Canterbury-Bankstown revival under coach Cameron Ciraldo, helping return the Bulldogs to the finals for the first time in eight years
clue_5: Still in his mid-20s, he twice signed contract extensions with the club, committing his long-term future to Belmore through to the end of 2028
clue_6: Canterbury-Bankstown Bulldogs winger and utility back (2022-present), a Lebanon international and Berala Bears junior who has become one of the Bulldogs' most popular modern players since his 2022 debut
facts: Kiraz is of Lebanese heritage and a devout Maronite Catholic. He made his international debut for Lebanon at just 17 years of age, against Fiji in June 2019, years before he played a single NRL game.
He represented Lebanon at the 2021 Rugby League World Cup, playing fullback and scoring against Ireland as the Cedars reached the quarter-finals.
He was named in Lebanon's squad for the 2019 World Cup Nines but was sent home after a single match, ruled ineligible because the tournament required players to be at least 18.

clue_1: The youngest of four sons of a Queensland railway worker, he grew up in a working-class city west of Brisbane and was playing first-grade football for his hometown club as a teenager in the mid-1980s
clue_2: Standing just 165 centimetres tall, he was one of the smallest men ever to dominate his position: a cheeky, darting playmaker whose lack of size belied a fearless running game and a knack for lifting big teams in the biggest moments
clue_3: In 1992 he completed a remarkable individual sweep, claiming the Clive Churchill Medal as the best player in the grand final and the Rothmans Medal as the season's best-and-fairest, and he later added the 1996 Dally M Medal
clue_4: He was the on-field general of the Brisbane Broncos' dynasty under Wayne Bennett, steering the club to four premierships during the 1990s
clue_5: After a stint in the English Super League, he was sensationally recalled to the Queensland State of Origin side in 2001, in his mid-30s, flying back from England to inspire one of the most famous series victories in the contest's history
clue_6: Brisbane Broncos halfback nicknamed 'Alfie', a four-time premiership winner and 1996 Dally M medallist who captained both Queensland and Australia and played 34 State of Origin games for the Maroons
facts: At the height of his fame in 1992, Langer starred in television advertisements for a major Australian bread brand alongside his own mother, and toy shops sold an official 'Alfie' doll made in his likeness.
He was named the Broncos' Player of the Year a club-record five times, and the Ipswich Jets' annual best-player award, the Allan Langer Medal, is named after him.
Langer was made a Member of the Order of Australia in 2000 for his service to rugby league, and in 2008 was named in the game's official list of the 100 Greatest Players.

clue_1: He grew up in the Hawke's Bay region of New Zealand's North Island, playing rugby union at boarding school, and only switched to rugby league as a teenager after a development officer spotted his potential
clue_2: A quietly spoken, relentlessly durable forward who shunned the spotlight, he built his reputation on enormous tackle counts and on almost never missing a match, the very model of a one-club workhorse
clue_3: He was named his club's Player of the Year in 2008 after appearing in every one of its 26 matches that season, and he would go on to captain both his club and his country
clue_4: He captained the New Zealand Warriors to the 2011 NRL Grand Final, where they were beaten 24-10 by Manly, the closest he ever came to a premiership
clue_5: When he retired at the end of the 2018 season, he did so as the most-capped player in the entire history of the Warriors, a true one-club man
clue_6: New Zealand Warriors second-rower and lock (2005-2018) who played a club-record 301 NRL games and led the side to the 2011 grand final, remembered as one of the most respected forwards of his era
facts: Mannering made his NRL debut in 2005 against the Brisbane Broncos, in the match that marked the Warriors' 10th anniversary in the competition.
He played 45 Tests for the New Zealand Kiwis and was part of the squad that stunned Australia to win the 2008 Rugby League World Cup, scoring two tries against Papua New Guinea during the tournament.
He was appointed captain of the Kiwis in 2013, taking over the role from Benji Marshall, and held the job until 2016.

clue_1: A dual Australian Schoolboys representative in the early 1980s, he made his first-grade debut at fullback in 1983 while still a teenager, and would go on playing right through until the 2000 season
clue_2: Blessed with searing pace and a famous head of curly hair, he was equally dangerous at fullback, in the centres or on the wing, and became one of the most prolific try-scorers the Australian game had seen, yet he never played in a winning grand final side
clue_3: He scored 165 tries for his club, a club record, and added 14 tries in 29 Tests for Australia across the late 1980s and 1990s
clue_4: A one-club man at the Cronulla-Sutherland Sharks, he captained the side to the 1997 Super League Grand Final, where they were beaten by the Brisbane Broncos
clue_5: After hanging up the boots in 2000, he became a familiar face on Australian television, hosting a long-running fishing and outdoor-adventure series and later appearing as a contestant on Australian Survivor
clue_6: Cronulla-Sutherland Sharks fullback and centre nicknamed 'ET' who played a then-record 328 games for the one club between 1983 and 2000, an NRL Hall of Fame inductee and one of the Sharks' inaugural club immortals
facts: In the early 1990s a magazine published a nude photograph of Ettingshausen, secretly taken in a shower during the 1990 Kangaroo Tour. He sued for defamation and won, in one of Australian sport's most famous privacy cases.
He played 27 State of Origin matches for New South Wales, and remains the only Kangaroo tourist ever to finish as the leading try-scorer on two consecutive tours, with 15 tries on each.

Although he toured with the Kangaroos twice and was one of his era's great finishers, Ettingshausen never played in a Rugby League World Cup: he was overlooked in 1988, ruled out by injury in 1992, and left out in 1995 during the Super League war.

clue_1: He came through the Newcastle junior system in the mid-1990s, and in 1997 spent a single season at a short-lived club that existed for just one year, one that travelled to England to contest a World Club Championship
clue_2: A small, pesky halfback with a razor-sharp kicking game, he became one of the great football journeymen, serving as the first-choice playmaker at five different clubs across a 16-season career
clue_3: He was named the competition's best halfback of 2000, and won a Clive Churchill Medal as the best player on the field in a grand final
clue_4: That grand final was the 1999 decider, when he steered the Melbourne Storm to a famous premiership in only the club's second season in the competition
clue_5: He wound down his playing career with two seasons at Canterbury, retiring in 2010, and is now a well-known voice in NRL television commentary
clue_6: Halfback nicknamed 'Noddy' who played 307 NRL games for the Newcastle Knights, Melbourne Storm, Northern Eagles, Cronulla Sharks and Canterbury Bulldogs, won the 1999 premiership and Clive Churchill Medal, and represented both New South Wales and Australia
facts: Kimmorley played 20 Tests for Australia, including at the 2000 Rugby League World Cup, and turned out 10 times for New South Wales in State of Origin.

He set up the most famous moment of the 1999 grand final himself: his late cross-field kick was caught by Craig Smith, who was knocked out by a high tackle as the ball spilled loose, leading the referee to award the controversial penalty try that won Melbourne the title.

After retiring he moved into coaching, working as an assistant at the Bulldogs and Canberra, taking caretaker charge of the Wests Tigers' NRL side in 2022, and later coaching the Wests Tigers in the women's premiership.

clue_1: Born in Sydney's eastern suburbs in 1982, he was a teenage prodigy who reached first grade at 18. His uncle was a celebrated South Sydney player who later led the famous public campaign to save that club from extinction
clue_2: A goal-kicking five-eighth and lock, he was one of the most marketable young faces of the game in the early 2000s, appearing on magazine covers and in the gossip columns as often as on the back pages
clue_3: He was named Rookie of the Year in 2001 and, four years later, the competition's best five-eighth, and he had already won a premiership at just 22 years of age
clue_4: That premiership came with the Canterbury-Bankstown Bulldogs in 2004, in a tense grand final won 16-13 against the very club he would later go on to captain
clue_5: He led the Sydney Roosters to the 2010 grand final and finished his playing career at the Wests Tigers, before reinventing himself as the host of a prime-time NRL television show
clue_6: Five-eighth and lock who played 288 NRL games for the Canterbury Bulldogs, Sydney Roosters and Wests Tigers, won the 2004 premiership as a 22-year-old, captained the Roosters, and now hosts the television show NRL 360
facts: Anasta is of Greek heritage through his father. In 2013 he played a single Test match for Greece, and in that one game scored four tries and kicked 15 goals for a personal haul of 46 points.
He represented New South Wales in 10 State of Origin matches and played four Tests for Australia, all of them in 2001.
After retiring in 2014, Anasta founded a player-management company, and now works at the same time as a television commentator and as an agent representing professional rugby league players.

clue_1: Born in Wellington, New Zealand, he moved to Australia's Gold Coast as a young boy and came through the junior ranks there, even spending time in a Sydney club's junior squad before signing his first professional contract
clue_2: He spent the early years of his career as a fullback drifting between clubs, managing only a handful of first-grade appearances across several seasons, before a change of position in his mid-20s completely transformed his career
clue_3: After moving to Melbourne he was converted from fullback to halfback, eventually taking on the number seven jersey once worn by one of the game's all-time-great playmakers
clue_4: He was the starting halfback when the Melbourne Storm won the 2020 NRL premiership, defeating Penrith in the grand final
clue_5: In 2024 he reached the peak of the game as an individual, steering an injury-hit Melbourne side to the minor premiership and being recognised as the competition's best player
clue_6: Melbourne Storm halfback, earlier of the Gold Coast Titans and North Queensland Cowboys, who won the 2020 premiership, claimed the 2024 Dally M Medal, and represents the New Zealand Kiwis
facts: Hughes endured one of the slowest starts of any modern NRL star: he played just one first-grade game in his 2013 debut season for the Gold Coast, and did not play another NRL match until 2016 with North Queensland.
He plays his international football for the New Zealand Kiwis, making his Test debut in 2019 with a try against Tonga, and was named the Kiwis' Player of the Year in 2021.
In 2025 Hughes re-signed with Melbourne on a contract running until 2030, and the Storm again reached the grand final, losing the 2025 decider to the Brisbane Broncos.
